title: "1. Carbon Pricing"
aliases:
  - ../research/1-carbon-pricing.html
---

Carbon prices stay low in open economies because one instrument is asked to do two jobs: to make producers cut emissions per unit of output, and to make consumers pay for the carbon in what they buy. A tax on domestic production charges exporters and spares imports, so governments exempt industry and hold the rate down. This section of papers gives each job its own instrument. A revenue-neutral feebate prices production intensity at the full rate at the margin, at no cost to the treasury. A carbon component of VAT and a forward obligation on energy suppliers price consumption, imports included. The Total Effective Carbon Price puts any instrument, priced or not, on one scale, so that border mechanisms, such as the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), and international payments can recognize policies rather than payments. In a stylized steel sector a feebate raises the price by \$15 per tonne where a tax at the same rate raises it by \$85; an international payment above half the feebate rate makes adoption a net gain; and once importers charge for embodied carbon, each exporter's most competitive feebate rate equals the charge in its markets.

## 1.1 Price Production and Consumption Separately {#paper-1-1}

*A Two-Track Architecture for Carbon Pricing in Open Economies*

Carbon prices stay low in open economies because one instrument does two jobs: it pushes producers to cut emissions per unit of output, and it makes buyers pay for the carbon they use. The second job hurts exporters and spares imports. This brief gives each job its own instrument. A revenue-neutral feebate prices production at no cost to the treasury and with a small price effect. A carbon component of VAT, and forward obligations on fuel suppliers, price consumption, imports included. Climate finance above half the feebate rate makes adoption a gain, and border charges set by country turn leakage into a race to the top.

## 1.2 Feebates: The Full Carbon Price at the Margin, Without the Carbon Bill {#paper-1-2}

*Decarbonizing Coal-Heavy Power and Trade-Exposed Industry*

Carbon taxes stall where coal dominates power or where industry competes abroad, because the tax charges producers for every tonne they still emit, not only for the tonnes they could avoid. A revenue-neutral feebate charges producers above a sector benchmark of emissions per unit of output and rebates those below it. It gives the same incentive to switch as a tax at the same rate but leaves average costs almost unchanged. In a stylized coal-heavy grid at \$50 per tonne, a tax raises average generation cost by 87 percent; a feebate raises it by nothing at the outset. Governments should use feebates where carbon taxes stall.

## 1.3 Converting a VAT into a Destination Carbon Tax {#paper-1-3}

*A Carbon Component in VAT and a Forward Obligation on Energy Suppliers in the European Union*

The EU prices the carbon its factories and power plants emit but barely prices the carbon in what Europeans buy, much of it emitted abroad. This brief proposes a carbon consumption tax in two parts. A carbon component of VAT charges every good consumed in the EU, imported or domestic, for its embodied carbon while the value component of VAT falls; exports are zero-rated and imports start on generous, rebuttable default intensities. A legal obligation announced a decade ahead makes the few large suppliers of road and heating fuel pay for the carbon they sell. The VAT part probably needs unanimity; the obligation does not.

## 1.4 Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment {#paper-1-4}

*Carbon Price Recognition and Scrap Shuffling under the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism*

The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) cuts an importer's charge by the carbon price the exporter has effectively paid, installation by installation. Two flaws follow. Instruments that send a full price signal but pay little net, such as feebates, rebated carbon taxes and energy subsidy reform, earn no credit. And exporters can ship scrap-based steel to the EU and blast-furnace steel elsewhere, cutting reported embodied carbon by three quarters in a stylized case with no fall in emissions. Measuring the price signal at country-sector level fixes both. The Commission should publish its default carbon price methodology and build these changes into the 2027 default-value revision.
